clinicalPearls: Typically affects young, myopic Caucasian men in the third to fourth decade, in contrast to the older demographic of primary open-angle glaucoma.

The classic triad is Krukenberg spindle (vertical pigment deposition on corneal endothelium), mid-peripheral iris transillumination defects in a radial spoke-like pattern, and heavy homogeneous trabecular meshwork pigmentation.
Reverse pupillary block, in which the peripheral iris bows posteriorly against the zonules and lens, is the leading mechanism for iridozonular chafing and pigment liberation.
Exercise or pupillary dilatation can precipitate a shower of pigment with an acute intraocular pressure spike, sometimes with corneal oedema and blurring.
Not all patients with pigment dispersion syndrome develop glaucoma; conversion to glaucoma occurs in a minority over time and warrants ongoing surveillance.
Laser peripheral iridotomy aims to flatten the iris and abolish reverse pupillary block, though evidence for preventing progression is inconsistent.
Pilocarpine addresses both pressure and iris configuration by pulling the iris away from the zonules, but is poorly tolerated in young myopes because of induced myopia and retinal detachment risk.
Laser trabeculoplasty is often effective given the heavily pigmented meshwork, but lower energy is prudent to avoid a marked post-laser pressure spike.
reference.pathophysiology: Mechanical rubbing of the posterior iris pigment epithelium against the anterior packets of lens zonules liberates melanin granules into the aqueous. A posteriorly bowed, concave peripheral iris configuration, driven by reverse pupillary block where aqueous is trapped in the anterior chamber and raises its pressure relative to the posterior chamber, brings the iris into contact with the zonules during physiological pupil movement. Dispersed pigment is carried by aqueous convection currents and deposited throughout the anterior segment, most importantly within the trabecular meshwork. Phagocytosis of pigment by trabecular endothelial cells, subsequent cell death, meshwork collapse and sclerosis progressively reduce aqueous outflow facility, elevating intraocular pressure and producing a glaucomatous optic neuropathy identical in appearance to primary open-angle glaucoma.
additionalDifferentials: pigment dispersion from a malpositioned posterior chamber intraocular lens
melanomalytic glaucoma from a pigmented iris or ciliary body tumour
additionalInvestigations: gonioscopy demonstrating dense homogeneous trabecular pigment and a concave peripheral iris
slit-lamp examination for Krukenberg spindle and iris transillumination defects
anterior segment optical coherence tomography or ultrasound biomicroscopy showing posterior iris bowing
diurnal intraocular pressure phasing to capture exercise or dilatation-related spikes
standard automated perimetry for glaucomatous field loss
optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell complex
optic disc stereo-photography for baseline documentation
redFlags: acute intraocular pressure spike after exercise or pupil dilatation with corneal oedema and haloes
progressive optic disc cupping or nerve fibre layer thinning despite treatment
markedly asymmetric pressures or pigmentation suggesting an alternative intraocular tumour
very high presenting pressures in a young myope at risk of rapid field loss
reference.prognosis: With early detection and pressure control the long-term visual prognosis is generally good, and pigment dispersion tends to diminish with age as the lens enlarges and the iris configuration flattens. Untreated or poorly controlled disease can progress to significant glaucomatous field loss and irreversible visual impairment.
pitfalls: Attributing a young myope's raised pressure to primary open-angle glaucoma and missing the diagnostic anterior segment signs.
Prescribing standard-energy laser trabeculoplasty without anticipating an exaggerated post-laser pressure spike in a heavily pigmented meshwork.
Overlooking exercise-induced pressure spikes because a single clinic reading is normal.
Using pilocarpine in a young high myope without counselling about induced myopia and the risk of retinal detachment.
Assuming all pigment dispersion syndrome will convert to glaucoma and over-treating patients who only require monitoring.

management: Initiate intraocular pressure-lowering topical therapy, usually a prostaglandin analogue, with adjunctive beta-blockers, alpha-agonists or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors for adequate control
Offer laser peripheral iridotomy to flatten the posteriorly bowed iris and interrupt reverse pupillary block driving pigment liberation
Apply laser trabeculoplasty judiciously given dense meshwork pigmentation and the risk of a marked post-laser pressure rise
Counsel patients to avoid strenuous exercise and situations causing pupillary dilatation that can trigger acute pigment-release pressure spikes
Proceed to filtration surgery or a drainage device when pressure remains uncontrolled or field loss progresses despite maximal therapy
Undertake ongoing surveillance with diurnal pressure phasing, gonioscopy, retinal nerve fibre layer OCT and perimetry, as only a minority with pigment dispersion convert to glaucoma
